title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Weak Duality: Proof

Let \(f\) be any flow, and let \((A, B)\) be any \(s-t\) cut. Then \(|f| \le cap(A, B)\).


Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
|f| &= \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} f(e) - \sum_{e \text{ in to } A} f(e) \\
    &\le \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} f(e) \qquad (\text{since } \sum_{e \text{ in to } A} f(e) \ge 0) \\
    &\le \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} c(e) \qquad (\text{since } f(e) \le c(e)) \\
    &= cap(A, B).
\end{aligned}
\]

This gives us a certificate of optimality: if we find a flow and a cut with equal value, both are optimal.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

If \(f\) is a flow in a flow network \(G = (V, E)\) with source \(s\) and sink \(t\), then the following conditions are equivalent:


\(f\) is a maximum flow in \(G\)




The residual network \(G_f\) contains no augmenting paths




\(|f| = cap(S, T)\) for some cut \((S, T)\) with \(s \in S,\ t \in T\)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Proof: \((1) \implies (2)\)

Proof. Suppose for contradiction that \(f\) is a maximum flow but \(G_f\) has an augmenting path \(p\).


Let \(c_f(p) = \min\{c_f(e) : e \in p\} > 0\) be the residual capacity along \(p\).




Augment \(f\) by \(c_f(p)\) units along \(p\) to get a new flow \(f'\)




Then \(|f'| = |f| + c_f(p) > |f|\), contradicting maximality of \(f\).


Thus a maximum flow cannot have any augmenting paths. ◻

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Proof: \((2) \implies (3)\)

Proof. Suppose \(G_f\) has no augmenting path, i.e., no path from \(s\) to \(t\) in \(G_f\).
Define \(S = \{v \in V : \text{there is a path from } s \text{ to } v \text{ in } G_f\}\) and \(T = V \setminus S\).


\(s \in S\), \(t \notin S\) (no \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(G_f\)), so \((S,T)\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut.




For any \(u \in S\), \(v \in T\):

If \((u,v) \in E\), then \(f(u,v) = c(u,v)\) (otherwise \((u,v) \in E_f\), placing \(v\) in \(S\))
If \((v,u) \in E\), then \(f(v,u) = 0\) (otherwise \(c_f(u,v) > 0\), placing \(v\) in \(S\))





Therefore: \(f(S,T) = \sum_{u\in S}\sum_{v\in T} c(u,v) = c(S,T)\), so \(|f| = cap(S,T)\). ◻

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Proof: \((3) \implies (1)\)

Proof. If \(|f| = cap(S,T)\) for some cut, then by weak duality:
\[|f| = cap(S,T) \ge \text{value of any flow}\]
So \(f\) must be a maximum flow. ◻

The three equivalences together form the Max Flow Min Cut Theorem — one of the most beautiful duality results in combinatorial optimization.

A technique to formalize that one problem is not “harder” than another.

\(D_1 \le_p D_2\) if there is a function \(f\) computable in polynomial time such that for all inputs \(x\): \[x \in D_1 \iff f(x) \in D_2\]

Decision problem \(D\) is NP-Complete if: 1. \(D\) is in NP 2. \(D\) is NP-hard: for all \(D'\) in NP, \(D' \le_p D\)

Cook’s Theorem (1971): SAT (Boolean satisfiability) is NP-complete — the first problem proven NP-complete.

All other NP-completeness proofs ultimately reduce from CIRCUIT-SAT or SAT. We’ll use 3-SAT as our starting point for most reductions.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Overview
The Cook-Levin Theorem (1971) established the first NP-complete problem.

Cook-Levin Theorem. SAT (Boolean formula satisfiability) is NP-complete.

Independent discovery by Stephen Cook (USA) and Leonid Levin (USSR). This theorem launched the field of NP-completeness.
Significance: It gives us a starting point for all other NP-completeness proofs.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Proof Strategy
Key insight: Any NP problem can be solved by a non-deterministic Turing Machine (NDTM) in polynomial time.
We will encode the entire computation of the NDTM as a Boolean formula that is satisfiable iff the NDTM accepts.
Ingredients: - A description of the NDTM for problem \(D\): \((Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{accept})\) where: - \(Q\) = states, \(\Sigma\) = input alphabet, \(\Gamma\) = tape alphabet - \(\delta\) = transition relation (non-deterministic) - \(q_0\) = start state, \(q_{accept}\) = accepting state

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Encoding the Computation
Given input \(x\) of length \(n\), the NDTM runs in time \(p(n)\) (polynomial).
We create Boolean variables to encode the computation:



Variable
Meaning




\(T[i,j,k]\)
Cell \(i\) of tape contains symbol \(k\) at time \(j\)


\(H[i,j]\)
Read/write head is at position \(i\) at time \(j\)


\(Q[q,j]\)
Machine is in state \(q\) at time \(j\)



Dimensions: - Tape cells: \(0\) to \(p(n)\) (the TM never uses more) - Time steps: \(0\) to \(p(n)\) - Symbols: finite alphabet \(\Gamma\) - States: finite set \(Q\)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Transition Constraints
The transition constraint is the core of the proof.
For each time \(t\), position \(i\), each combination of state \(q\) and tape symbol \(s\):

Look at the NDTM’s transition relation \(\delta(q, s)\)
For each possible next move \((q', s', d)\) (where \(d \in \{L, R\}\)):

New state: \(Q[q', t+1]\)
New symbol: \(T[i, t+1, s']\)
Head moved: \(H[i + d, t+1]\)


This creates a CNF clause saying: if at time \(t\), the head is at \(i\), state is \(q\), and symbol is \(s\), then at time \(t+1\), the configuration must be consistent with some valid transition.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Formula Size
The resulting formula \(\phi\) has size \(O(p(n)^3)\):

\(O(p(n)^2)\) cells \(\times\) \(O(p(n))\) time steps = \(O(p(n)^3)\) variables
Each constraint is localized (involving nearby cells and adjacent time steps)
Total formula size is polynomial in \(n\) ✓

Correctness: - (\(\Rightarrow\)) If the NDTM accepts \(x\), the accepting computation gives a satisfying assignment - (\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(\phi\) is satisfiable, the assignment encodes a valid accepting computation of the NDTM

CLIQUE is NP-Complete

A clique is a complete subgraph — every pair of vertices is connected by an edge.

title: Tulasimohan Molli

text:
CLIQUE is NP-hard: Reduction from 3-SAT
Given a 3-CNF formula \(F\) with \(k\) clauses and variables \(x_1, \dots, x_n\):
Construct graph \(G\): - \(3k\) vertices — one triple \(T_c\) per clause \(c = (\ell_1 \lor \ell_2 \lor \ell_3)\){.fragment} - Label vertices in each triple by the literals of the corresponding clause{.fragment} - Add edges between every pair of vertices except:{.fragment} - Nodes in the same triple (no edges within a clause) - Nodes that are complementary (e.g., \(x_i\) and \(\overline{x_i}\))
Set \(k\) (clique size) = number of clauses.{.fragment}

Running time: \(O(|V| + |E|)\) — trivial! {.fragment}

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Terminology: Minimization Problems
For a minimization problem: - OPT\((I)\) = value of optimal solution for instance \(I\) - ALG\((I)\) = value computed by algorithm ALG for instance \(I\)

ALG is a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm if: \[\text{ALG}(I) \le \rho \cdot \text{OPT}(I) \quad \text{for all inputs } I\]
\(\rho\) is called the approximation factor.

Example: If ALG computes a vertex cover with at most twice the minimum vertices, then ALG is a 2-approximation.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Terminology: Maximization Problems
For a maximization problem:

ALG is a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm if: \[\text{ALG}(I) \ge \frac{1}{\rho} \cdot \text{OPT}(I) \quad \text{for all inputs } I\]

Example: If ALG finds a clique with at least half the maximum size, then ALG is a 2-approximation.
Note: \(\rho \ge 1\) always — smaller \(\rho\) means better approximation.

text:
Vertex Cover: The Problem

Given a graph \(G = (V, E)\), find a subset \(C \subseteq V\) such that for each edge \((u,v) \in E\), at least \(u\) or \(v\) is in \(C\).

Optimization problem: Find a vertex cover with minimum number of vertices.
Status: Vertex Cover is NP-hard (we proved the decision version is NP-complete).
We will design a 2-approximation algorithm.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Vertex Cover: Naive Greedy
Greedy strategy: Repeatedly pick a vertex of highest degree and remove all incident edges.
Problem: Might select wrong vertices, leading to bad approximation.
Example: A star graph + many isolated edges. Greedy might pick the center (good) but in other cases picks poorly.






Warning


The approximation ratio of this simple greedy can be as bad as \(\Theta(\log n)\) — or even \(|V| - 1\) in constructed worst cases.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Vertex Cover: 2-Approximation
APPROX-VERTEX-COVER algorithm: - While there are edges in \(G\): 1. Pick any edge \((u,v)\) from \(G\) 2. Add both \(u\) and \(v\) to the cover 3. Remove all edges incident to \(u\) or \(v\) from \(G\)

APPROX-VERTEX-COVER is a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Set Cover Problem

Set Cover: - Input: A finite set \(X\) (universe) and a family \(F\) of subsets of \(X\), such that every element of \(X\) belongs to at least one subset in \(F\) - Goal: Find a minimum-size subfamily \(S \subseteq F\) that covers all elements of \(X\)

Status: Set Cover is NP-hard — it is a generalization of Vertex Cover.
Applications: - Network discovery - Hitting set problems - Emergency facility location

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Set Cover: Greedy Approximation
Greedy choice: At each stage, pick the set that covers the most uncovered elements.

The greedy heuristic achieves an approximation factor of \(\ln m\), where \(m = |X|\) is the total number of elements.

Proof idea (pigeonhole principle): - Let \(c\) be the optimal cover size - At each step, some set in the optimal cover covers at least \(1/c\) of the remaining uncovered elements - Greedy picks a set covering at least as many - After \(g\) rounds: uncovered \(\le m \cdot (1 - 1/c)^g \le m \cdot e^{-g/c}\) - When \(m \cdot e^{-g/c} < 1\), all covered → \(g \ge c \ln m\)

text:

Network Discovery Problem: Find the topology of a network using a minimal number of queries about edges connected to a vertex.
Hitting Set Problem: Given a set of unit rectangles (representing coverage areas), hit all rectangles with minimum number of points.
Variant: Weighted Set Cover — each set has a cost, goal is to minimize total cost of selected sets.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Greedy Set Cover: Analysis
Let: - \(c\) be the size of the optimal set cover (OPT) - \(g\) be the size of the greedy set cover (ALG)
Let \(m_0 = m\) be the initial number of uncovered elements. Let \(m_i\) be the number remaining after \(i\) iterations.
After \(i-1\) rounds, \(m_{i-1}\) elements remain. Since there is a cover of size \(c\), by the pigeonhole principle, some set covers at least \(m_{i-1} / c\) elements.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Greedy Set Cover: Recurrence
Greedy picks the largest set, so it covers at least \(m_{i-1} / c\) elements in iteration \(i\):
\[m_i \le m_{i-1} - \frac{m_{i-1}}{c} = m_{i-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{c}\right)\]
Unrolling the recurrence:
\[m_i \le m \left(1 - \frac{1}{c}\right)^i\]

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Greedy Set Cover: Final Bound
Using \(1 - x \le e^{-x}\):
\[m_i \le m \cdot e^{-i/c}\]
After \(g\) iterations (the greedy cover size), all elements are covered (\(m_g < 1\)):
\[m \cdot e^{-g/c} < 1\]
Solving for \(g\): \[e^{-g/c} < 1/m \quad\Rightarrow\quad -g/c < -\ln m \quad\Rightarrow\quad g > c \ln m\]

\[|\text{GREEDY}| \le |\text{OPT}| \cdot \ln m\]

title: Tulasimohan Molli
section: Is the Greedy Set Cover Bound Tight?
text:
Is the Greedy Set Cover Bound Tight?
Yes! There exist instances where the greedy ratio is \(\Omega(\log n)\).
Example: Construct a bipartite-like set system where: - OPT = 2 - Greedy picks \(\Theta(\log n)\) sets
Hardness: For every \(\epsilon > 0\), Set Cover cannot be approximated within \((1-\epsilon)\ln m\) unless P = NP.
So the greedy bound is essentially optimal for this problem!

Greedy variant: Pick the set that minimizes cost per newly covered element: \[\frac{w(S)}{|S \cap \text{uncovered}|}\]
Analysis: Same approximation factor \(\ln m\).
Application: Facility location — each potential facility has a cost, each facility covers a region. Minimize cost to cover all demand points.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP)
Problem: Given a set of cities along with the cost of travel between them, find the cheapest route visiting all cities and returning to the starting point.

Formal Definition: Given a complete undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with nonnegative integer cost \(c(u,v)\) for each edge \((u,v) \in E\), find a Hamiltonian cycle of \(G\) with minimum cost.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
TSP Variants
Metric TSP: Costs satisfy the triangle inequality: \[c(u,w) \le c(u,v) + c(v,w) \quad \text{for all } u,v,w \in V\]
Euclidean TSP: Cities are points in Euclidean space, costs equal to Euclidean distance.
General TSP: No restriction on costs — can be arbitrarily assigned.






Important


General TSP is much harder to approximate than Metric TSP!

title: Tulasimohan Molli
Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Metric TSP: Approximation Algorithm
Idea: First compute an MST, then create a tour based on the tree.
APPROX-TSP-TOUR: 1. Compute a minimum spanning tree \(T_{\min}\) of \(G\){.fragment} 2. Let \(W\) be a full walk of \(T_{\min}\) (traverses each edge twice){.fragment} 3. Remove duplicate vertices from \(W\) to obtain a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\){.fragment}
Runtime: Dominated by MST-PRIM — \(\Theta(V^2)\).

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Full Walk vs. Hamiltonian Cycle
Full walk: Starting from root, do a DFS, listing each vertex when visited (including on backtrack). Each edge traversed twice.
Shortcutting: Remove duplicates (keeping only the first occurrence) to get a Hamiltonian cycle. By triangle inequality, this only reduces cost.

Walk: \(a \to b \to c \to b \to d \to b \to a \to e \to a\) Ham cycle: \(a \to b \to c \to d \to e \to a\)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Visual Proof Sketch

Optimal tour \(H^*\) (cost = OPT)
Remove one edge from \(H^*\) → spanning tree \(T\) (cost \(\le\) OPT)
Minimum spanning tree \(T_{\min}\) (cost \(\le\) cost of \(T\))
Full walk \(W\) of \(T_{\min}\) (traverses each edge twice: cost \(= 2c(T_{\min}) \le 2\cdot\) OPT)
Shortcut duplicates from \(W\) to get tour \(H\) (cost \(\le\) cost of \(W\) by triangle inequality)

Thus \(c(H) \le 2 \cdot \text{OPT}\). ◻

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Improving the Bound
The MST-based 2-approximation can be improved:
Christofides’ Algorithm (1976): 1. Compute MST \(T_{\min}\) 2. Find minimum-weight perfect matching \(M\) on odd-degree vertices of \(T_{\min}\) 3. Eulerian tour on \(T_{\min} \cup M\) 4. Shortcut to get Hamiltonian cycle
Result: 1.5-approximation for Metric TSP — best known polynomial-time guarantee.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
What is Backtracking?
Backtracking is a systematic method for exploring all possible solutions to a problem by incrementally building candidates and abandoning (“backtracking” from) partial candidates that cannot be completed to a valid solution.
Key idea: Prune the search space as early as possible.
Applications: - Constraint satisfaction problems (n-Queens, Sudoku) - Combinatorial optimization (Knapsack, TSP) - Graph problems (Hamiltonian Cycle, Graph Coloring) - Puzzles (crosswords, maze solving)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Example: n-Queens Problem
Problem: Place \(n\) queens on an \(n \times n\) chessboard so that no two queens attack each other.
Constraints: - No two queens share the same row - No two queens share the same column - No two queens share the same diagonal
State: Queens placed in first \(k\) rows Extensions: Which column to place the \((k+1)\)-th queen?

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
n-Queens: Pruning
Basic backtracking: Try placing a queen in each column, check if valid, and backtrack if stuck.
Forward checking: Before placing, compute which positions are still available.
Constraint propagation: Use arc consistency to deduce forced placements.
4-Queens backtracking tree.
The pruning is so effective that the 8-Queens problem has only 92 solutions out of \(\binom{64}{8} \approx 4.4 \times 10^9\) possible placements.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Backtracking: Worst-Case Analysis
Without pruning: Backtracking explores the entire search tree — potentially exponential.

n-Queens naive: \(\binom{n^2}{n}\) possibilities
n-Queens with row/column constraints: \(n!\) possibilities

With pruning: Often much faster in practice, but worst case remains exponential.
When is backtracking useful? - Problem is NP-hard (no polynomial algorithm known) - Instance sizes are moderate (\(n \le 20-100\)) - Good pruning rules are available

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Hamiltonian Cycle via Backtracking
Problem: Given a graph \(G = (V, E)\), find a cycle visiting all vertices exactly once.
Backtracking approach: 1. Start with vertex \(v_0\), mark it visited{.fragment} 2. Try to extend the path to an unvisited neighbor{.fragment} 3. If path has \(|V|\) vertices and the last vertex connects to \(v_0\), a Hamiltonian cycle is found{.fragment} 4. If no unvisited neighbor exists, backtrack{.fragment}
Pruning heuristics: - Degree-1 vertices: if a vertex has degree \(< 2\), no cycle possible - Connected components: if removing a visited vertex disconnects unvisited vertices, prune

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Subset Sum / Knapsack via Backtracking
Problem: Given items with weights \(w_i\) and values \(v_i\), find a subset of maximum total value with total weight \(\le W\).
Backtracking tree: - At each level \(i\), decide whether to include item \(i\) - State: current weight \(w\), current value \(v\), item index \(i\)
Pruning: - If \(w + w_i > W\), skip (infeasible) - If \(v + \text{optimistic\_future} < \text{best\_so\_far}\), prune (bound)
This is the Branch and Bound approach — covered in the next lecture!

Bounding Functions
The quality of B&B depends on tight bounds:
For minimization problems: - Lower bound: An optimistic estimate of the minimum solution within the subproblem (must be \(\le\) true optimum) - Upper bound: The best solution found so far (prunes subproblems whose LB exceeds this)
For maximization problems: - Upper bound: An optimistic estimate of the maximum solution (must be \(\ge\) true optimum) - Lower bound: The best solution found so far






Important


Tighter bounds = more pruning = faster search. Design of good bounds is both an art and a science.

text:
Example: 0-1 Knapsack
Problem: Maximize \(\sum v_i x_i\) subject to \(\sum w_i x_i \le W\), \(x_i \in \{0,1\}\).
Branching: At each level, decide to include or exclude an item.
Upper bound (optimistic): Relax integrality — allow fractional items (greedy by \(v_i/w_i\)): - Sort items by \(v_i/w_i\) descending - Take items fully while possible, then take a fraction of the next - This gives an upper bound on the optimal integer solution
Pruning: If the upper bound \(\le\) best found so far, prune.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Knapsack B&B: Example
Items: \((v_i, w_i)\): A=(40,2), B=(30,3), C=(50,5), D=(10,1), \(W=7\)
Greedy order: D (10), A (20), B (10), C (10) — by \(v_i/w_i\)
Step 1: Root: take all = 130, but over weight. Fractional: D+A+B + \(\frac{1}{5}\)C = 90. Upper bound = 90.
Branch on D: - Take D: weight=1, value=10. Remaining capacity=6. Upper bound on children: 10 + fractional of A,B,C = 10+40+30+0 = 80 - Skip D: weight=0, value=0. Upper bound: 0 + fractional of A,B,C = 40+30+50 = 120 (but wait — A+B+\(\frac{2}{5}\)C with \(W=7\): A(40) + B(30) + \(\frac{2}{5}\)C(20) = 90)

Knapsack B&B: Search Tree
Knapsack B&B search tree.
Pruning rules: - UB \(\le\) best integer solution found → prune - Infeasible (weight \(> W\)) → prune - All items considered → leaf (update best)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Traveling Salesman via B&B
Problem: Minimize tour cost visiting all cities.
Lower bound (assignment relaxation): - A tour consists of \(n\) edges, one entering and one leaving each city - Relax the “single cycle” requirement — we get a minimum weight assignment problem (a set of cycles covering all cities) - Solve in \(O(n^3)\) via Hungarian algorithm - This is a lower bound on the optimal TSP tour
Branching: Pick a subtour (cycle of length \(< n\)) and branch by excluding an edge from that cycle.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
TSP B&B: Lower Bound Example
TSP assignment relaxation.
Lower bound calculation: 1. Subtract row minima from each row 2. Subtract column minima from each column 3. Sum of all subtracted values = lower bound
Branching: On a subtour \((a,b,c,a)\), create branches: - Exclude \((a,b)\) - Exclude \((b,c)\) - Exclude \((c,a)\)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
What is Linear Programming?
Linear Programming (LP) is a powerful optimization framework for problems where both the objective and constraints are linear functions.

A linear program is an optimization problem of the form:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize} \quad & c^T x \\
\text{subject to} \quad & Ax \le b \\
& x \ge 0
\end{aligned}\]
where \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the vector of decision variables, \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(b \in \mathbb{R}^m\).

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Standard vs. Canonical Forms
Standard form: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize} \quad & c^T x \\
\text{subject to} \quad & Ax \le b \\
& x \ge 0
\end{aligned}\]
Canonical form (for simplex): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize} \quad & c^T x \\
\text{subject to} \quad & Ax = b \\
& x \ge 0
\end{aligned}\]
Conversion: Add slack variables \(s_i \ge 0\) to turn \(\le\) into \(=\): \[a_i^T x \le b_i \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_i^T x + s_i = b_i\]

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
The Simplex Algorithm
Geometric idea: Walk along edges of the feasible polytope from vertex to vertex, always improving the objective.
Simplex Algorithm: 1. Start at a basic feasible solution (a vertex) 2. Check if current vertex is optimal: - If all reduced costs \(\le 0\), stop (optimal found) 3. Move to a neighboring vertex with higher objective value 4. Repeat
Performance: Exponential worst-case (Klee-Minty), but polynomial on average and extremely fast in practice.

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Duality
Every LP has a dual LP that provides upper bounds on the primal optimum.
Primal (maximization): \[\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & c^T x \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & Ax \le b, \; x \ge 0
\end{aligned}\]
Dual (minimization): \[\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & b^T y \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & A^T y \ge c, \; y \ge 0
\end{aligned}\]

Weak Duality. For any feasible \(x\) (primal) and \(y\) (dual): \(c^T x \le b^T y\).


Strong Duality. If both primal and dual are feasible, their optimal values are equal: \(c^T x^* = b^T y^*\).

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
Duality: Economic Interpretation
Primal variables \(x_j\): Activity levels Dual variables \(y_i\): Shadow prices of resources
If a resource constraint is tight (slack = 0), its shadow price tells us how much the objective would improve if we had one more unit of that resource.
Complementary slackness: At optimality: - If \(x_j > 0\), then the \(j\)-th dual constraint is tight: \(a_j^T y = c_j\) - If \(y_i > 0\), then the \(i\)-th primal constraint is tight: \(a_i^T x = b_i\)

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
LP Applications in Algorithms
Network Flow as LP: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize} \quad & \sum_v f(s,v) \\
\text{subject to} \quad & 0 \le f(u,v) \le c(u,v) \\
& \sum_u f(u,v) - \sum_u f(v,u) = 0 \quad \forall v \ne s,t
\end{aligned}\]
Max flow is a linear program! The max flow = min cut theorem is a special case of LP strong duality.
Other algorithmic applications: - Minimum cost flow - Shortest path (LP formulation) - Bipartite matching - Multicommodity flow - Approximation algorithms via LP rounding

title: Tulasimohan Molli
text:
LP-Based Approximation Algorithms
LP is a powerful tool for designing approximation algorithms:
General approach: 1. Formulate the problem as an integer linear program (ILP) 2. Relax integrality to get an LP (polynomial-time solvable) 3. Solve the LP to get an optimal fractional solution 4. Round the fractional solution to an integer solution
Example: Vertex Cover ILP: \[\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{v \in V} x_v \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & x_u + x_v \ge 1 \quad \forall (u,v) \in E \\
& x_v \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}\]
LP relaxation: \(0 \le x_v \le 1\). Rounding: if \(x_v \ge 1/2\), set to 1 → 2-approximation!
